description_full: Revolve Group, Inc. operates as a fashion retailer for millennial and generation z consumers in the United States and internationally. The company operates in two segments, REVOLVE and FWRD. It operates a platform that connects consumers and global fashion influencers, as well as emerging, established, and owned brands. The company offers apparel, footwear, accessories, and beauty products from emerging, established, and owned brands, as well as luxury brands. It serves its customers through its websites, mobile applications, and stores. The company was formerly known as Advance Holdings, LLC and changed its name to Revolve Group, Inc. in October 2018. Revolve Group, Inc. was founded in 2003 and is headquartered in Cerritos, California.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 1K people. Revenue per employee of $737K ranks in the top quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers, improving at 13%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $29K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $6K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 1× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags elevated compensation governance risk (7/10).
financial_summary: Revolve Group, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $1.3B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 27% against a 12% cost of capital — a 16-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 54% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $48M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.96× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 0.2%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 6% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (8%).
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.73x).
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-10.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 42% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 50% and a beta of 1.45, it amplifies market moves, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.69 vs 5y 1.84), so read it loosely.
About $17.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 65% in the 2020 crash and 67% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $16.37 (margin of safety -13%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 44%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $11.76 to $24.11 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/FCF 27.5 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 50% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $30.31 on average, 64% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 27% clears the cost of capital of 11.9% by 16pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.77).
It runs a 54% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
ROE of 12% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.9% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $292.3M (22% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 6.4, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 130 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.6% over 3 years and 16.1% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 20%).
At current returns, reinvesting 100% of profits supports about 27.5% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -7.7% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 2.5x depreciation (0.9% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 13.1% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.7%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (22 sales, net $16.1M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 0.2% (0.2% in buybacks).
Short interest is elevated at 11.7% of the float, 5.5 days to cover.
people: With about 1,664 employees, each generates about $737K of revenue, 1.9x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 12.6% a year.
That works out to $29K of free cash flow per employee.
The company is founder-led, which often keeps management aligned with long-term owners.
CEO pay is $485K (1x revenue per employee).
